etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English dirti, alteration of earlier dritti, equivalent to dirt +‎ -y. Cognate with Middle Low German drēterich (“dirty”). See also drite.

definitions.definition: Unclean; covered with or containing unpleasant substances such as dirt or grime.

quote.citation: 1905, George Bernard Shaw, The author's apology from Mrs. Warren's Profession, page 61:
quote.text: Many persons are more comfortable when they are dirty than when they are clean; but that does not recommend dirt as a national policy.

definitions.definition: That makes one unclean; corrupting, infecting.
Morally unclean; obscene or indecent, especially sexually.

quote.citation: 2023 May 13, Kitty Drake, “This is how we do it: ‘A tired, throwaway midweek shag doesn’t interest me’”, in The Guardian‎[1], →ISSN:
quote.text: We have quite a playful and fun relationship in general, but it’s still surprising how dirty our sex can be in the things we say or do or pretend. We often laugh about it afterwards.

definitions.definition: Dishonorable; violating accepted standards or rules.

quote.citation: 1915, C.J. Dennis, The Songs of a Sentimental Bloke, published 1916, page 13:
quote.text: The world 'as got me snouted jist a treat; Crool Forchin's dirty left 'as smote me soul.

quote.citation: 2013 June 21, Oliver Burkeman, “The tao of tech”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 2, page 27:
quote.text: The dirty secret of the internet is that all this distraction and interruption is immensely profitable. […] Partly, this is a result of how online advertising has traditionally worked: advertisers pay for clicks, and a click is a click, however it's obtained.

definitions.definition: Corrupt, illegal, or improper.
Out of tune.
Of color, discolored by impurities.
(computing) Containing data needing to be written back to memory or disk.

quote.citation: 2008, Stephen R. G. Fraser, Real World ASP.NET: Building a Content Management System, page 105:
quote.text: Notice that an asterisk has been added to the filename in the edit window tabs. This is a simple reminder that the file is “dirty” and needs saving.

definitions.definition: (slang) Carrying illegal drugs among one's possessions or inside of one's bloodstream.
(informal) Used as an intensifier, especially in conjunction with "great".
Sleety; gusty; stormy.

quote.citation: 1867, Matthew Arnold, On the Study of Celtic Literature:
quote.text: Storms of wind, clouds of dust, an angry, dirty sea.

quote.citation: 1984, Douglas Adams, So Long, and Thanks for All the Fish (The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy):
quote.text: Rain type 17 was a dirty blatter battering against his windscreen so hard that it didn't make much odds whether he had his wipers on or off.

definitions.definition: (slang) Of an alcoholic beverage, especially a cocktail or mixed drink: served with the juice of olives.
Of food, indulgent in an unhealthy way.

quote.citation: 2003, Tom Christiansen, Nathan Torkington, Perl Cookbook, page xix:
quote.text: You can call it quick-and-dirty if you like, but there are billions of dollars out there riding on the supposition that fast food is not necessarily dirty food.

quote.citation: 2019, Oliver Berry, Fionn Davenport, Lonely Planet England:
quote.text: Piled high and oozing all the trimmings, the dirty burgers here are decidedly good – spice things up with jalapeños, brie or a seriously sticky BBQ sauce.

quote.citation: 2020, Mellissa Sevigny, Squeaky Clean Keto: Next Level Keto to Hack Your Health, Victory Belt Publishing, →ISBN, page 13:
quote.text: Dirty keto refers to an approach that follows the typical keto macro ratios, but the  components include “dirty” foods like fast food, packaged convenience foods,  processed meats, artificially sweetened diet sodas and sports drinks, and  unhealthy  […]

definitions.definition: Spreading harmful radiation over a wide area.
(aviation) Having the undercarriage or flaps in the down position.
In a dirty manner.
(transitive) To make (something) dirty.
(transitive) To stain or tarnish (somebody) with dishonor.
(transitive) To debase by distorting the real nature of (something).
(intransitive) To become soiled.

quote.citation: 1960 March, “Talking of Trains: S.R. signalling innovation”, in Trains Illustrated, page 135:
quote.text: The markers for the slow line signals have been arranged at cab level, but for the inner fast lines they have had to be kept low in the "six-foot", with the result that they tend to be badly dirtied by passing traffic.
